Let $y={e}^{\lambda x}.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+2\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+10{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +10) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +10=0.
$$

The auxiliary equation can be solved by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +10 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +1)-1+10 & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)^{2}+9 & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)^{2} & =-9 \\ \lambda +1 & =\pm 3\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =-1\pm 3\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={e}^{-x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡3x).\end{aligned}
$$

Now let's find the constants $P$ and $Q.$ 

Substituting $y\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)=1$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}Q{e}^{-\pi /6} & =1 \\ Q & ={e}^{\pi /6}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)=2.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}$:

$$
{y}^{′}=-{e}^{-x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡3x)+{e}^{-x}(-3P\operatorname{sin}⁡3x+3Q\operatorname{cos}⁡3x)
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)=2$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-Q{e}^{-\pi /6}-3P{e}^{-\pi /6} & =2 \\ -Q-3P & =2{e}^{\pi /6} \\ -{e}^{\pi /6}-3P & =2{e}^{\pi /6} \\ P & =-{e}^{\pi /6}.\end{aligned}
$$

So we have $Q={e}^{\pi /6}$ and $P=-{e}^{\pi /6}.$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={e}^{-x}(-{e}^{\pi /6}\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+{e}^{\pi /6}\operatorname{sin}⁡3x) \\  & ={e}^{-x+\pi /6}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+\operatorname{sin}⁡3x).\end{aligned}
$$

rationale: Completing lambda^2+2lambda+10 adds and subtracts1; the parenthesized lambda^2+2lambda+1 must not be squared a second time.
